title: OSF HealthCare physician highlights risks and safety tips for snowmobile season
text:
Paul Arco Media Relations Coordinato | OSF HealthCare, Featured Stories, IL
Paul Arco Media Relations Coordinato | OSF HealthCare, Featured Stories, IL
Every year, snowmobile accidents result in 14,000 injuries and nearly 200 deaths in the United States, according to data from the National Institutes of Health. Dr. John Bednar, an emergency room physician with OSF HealthCare, has seen a range of injuries caused by snowmobiling, from minor ankle sprains to severe trauma similar to what is observed in motorcycle accidents.
“Snowmobile crashes can be absolutely horrendous, life threatening and such a tragedy if you have an unexpected accident, like we see every year,” said Dr. Bednar. “Deaths, severe spinal injuries, pelvic fractures, multiple broken bones that can be devastating, devastating injuries and totally unexpected when you're out there to have fun.”
Dr. Bednar identified alcohol and drug use as the most significant risk factors in these incidents. “I've seen very few snowmobile accidents that did not have some sort of intoxication involved or other preventive kind of reckless behavior,” he stated. “Intoxication, number one, by far, seems to be most involved in the crashes I've seen over the decades.”
Another contributing factor is unfamiliarity with the terrain. Snowmobilers who travel outside their local areas are particularly at risk if they do not know the trails well. “Know your trail and stay on your trail,” Dr. Bednar advised. “If it's a well-known, well-marked trail, then you're much less likely to hit a stump, hit a rock, get off course, hit the tree, because that's when we see the crashes. When they don't know their trail, they use excessive speed, or they get off course, that's when they hit the tree or the rock, and those things don't like moving, and our heads don't like sudden stops.”
Dr. Bednar also emphasized controlling speed—especially for inexperienced riders or during nighttime when visibility is limited—and wearing proper protective gear such as helmets and body protection to reduce injury risk and prevent frostbite or hypothermia.
“Most snowmobilers have great gear, including their helmets,” he noted. “But if you are going to go on ice, if you think it is safe ice, please consider wearing a life vest underneath your gear. We’ve seen multiple tragedies on thin ice.”
The Michigan Department of Natural Resources recommends additional safety measures: dressing appropriately for weather conditions; checking forecasts and road status; carrying essential equipment such as flashlights and ice picks; having spare gear available; staying hydrated; riding with others; informing someone about your plans; using reliable communication devices in remote areas; and honestly assessing personal health before heading out.
OSF HealthCare is a nonprofit integrated health system serving Illinois and Michigan through hospitals and clinics focused on compassionate care according to its official website. The organization provides community health guidance—including seasonal safety tips—through its newsroom as part of its mission.
Whether for experienced riders or those new to snowmobiling this season, following these guidelines may help ensure safer experiences on snowy trails.
